counter.label: little animals in a drop of pepper-water, by his count

connections.why: That frame tells Leeuwenhoek's red blood cells of 1674 and how his single-lens microscopes were built; this one, the little animals he found with them two years later.
Oldenburg printed Leeuwenhoek's pepper-water letter in the Philosophical Transactions, the journal that frame describes, and the Society's fellows saw his animals for themselves in November 1677.

Leeuwenhoek's lens was a glass bead of the kind Hooke had described in the preface of Micrographia, and in 1677 Hooke's own single-lens microscope showed the Royal Society the creatures Leeuwenhoek reported.

Leeuwenhoek's single beads of glass were not surpassed for a century and a half, until achromatic object-glasses freed the compound microscope of the colored fringes that had kept it worse than a bead.
